chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Burayd ibn Mu'awiya from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

A man bought from another man ten thousand tons of reeds in Anbar, some upon some from a single pile, and Anbar contained thirty thousand tons. The seller said, 'I have sold you ten thousand tons of this reed.' The buyer said, 'I have accepted, bought, and agreed.' He gave him one thousand dirhams from its price, and the buyer appointed someone to take possession of it. In the morning, fire had fallen upon the reeds, and twenty thousand tons of it were burned, and ten thousand tons remained. He said, 'The ten thousand tons that remained are for the buyer, and the twenty thousand that were burned are from the property of the seller.'

key_terms.أَجَمَةٍ: Pile or heap (referring to the bulk storage)
key_terms.أَنْبَارٍ: Anbar (a historical city in Iraq known for its markets)
key_terms.قَصَبٍ: Reeds (a type of plant used for construction or weaving)

ai.seo_question: Who bears the risk of loss when part of a bulk commodity is destroyed by fire before separation in a Shia legal ruling?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *gharar* (uncertainty) in bulk sales (*kharaj bi-la wazn*), where risk allocation depends on the transfer of possession (*qabd*). The ruling that the seller bears the loss of the burned portion underscores the importance of actual or constructive possession in transferring ownership risk, a key distinction in Usuli jurisprudence compared to other schools.
